description: Software Engineering student and AI Infrastructure Lead with hands-on hackathon experience building multi-agent AI systems, scalable Go/Python backends, and cloud-native architectures. Looking to team up with driven frontend/mobile developers (React/Flutter) and UI/UX designers to ship an ambitious, high-impact project. Bring strong execution and problem-solving skills—let’s build something great!
summary:
KP Open Farm Atlas is the first public map of what grows where in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, which land is irrigated, and whether each union council’s crops received enough water in the last ten days. It was built for the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge (Peshawar).

The atlas computes a ten-day water deficit — actual crop water use minus rainfall — for every administrative unit in the province, using NASA POWER daily weather, ESA WorldCereal crop and irrigation maps, and ESA WorldCover cropland data. Each unit is classified green (no deficit), amber (1–30 mm gap), or red (above 30 mm). The map covers 31 districts and 122 tehsils, with drill-down to six-dekad time series charts, hectare breakdowns, and CSV/GeoJSON downloads per unit.

A scheduled GitHub Action re-runs the pipeline every Monday, commits updated data, and redeploys the static site — so the map stays current with zero server cost. The interface supports English, Urdu, and Pashto.

Pakistan has no public, sub-district crop water-balance map. Extension officers currently route field visits by who called last; this gives them a data-driven starting point. The atlas is honest about its limits: it says “union council, not farm” and “last ten days, not forecast.” Crop-area estimates are validated against the 2024 Agricultural Census, and disagreements are shown, not hidden.
details:
What it does:
The atlas shows 31 KP districts coloured green, amber, or red by ten-day water balance on an interactive Leaflet map. Users click a district to see its tehsils coloured by status or shaded by crop hectares, with a searchable list sorted driest-first and a trend arrow. Clicking a tehsil shows hectares of cropland, winter cereals, maize, and irrigated land; a six-dekad chart of crop water use vs. rainfall; the deficit in millimetres; a historical percentile comparing the current deficit to 2001–2025; and CSV/GeoJSON download. A play button animates six periods. Users can switch between plain map, satellite imagery, and terrain. A 3D globe view (Three.js) renders deficit as bar height. A built-in guide page explains the colours and vocabulary in English, Urdu, and Pashto. A methods page documents every dataset, threshold, and known weakness.

How it works:
A Python pipeline (no dependencies beyond requests, optional earthengine-api) runs four scripts:

  1. prepare_boundaries.py — downloads geoBoundaries KP districts and tehsils, assigns stable IDs.
  2. fetch_power.py — pulls NASA POWER daily precipitation and weather parameters per centroid, with disk caching and retries.
  3. build_series.py — computes FAO-56 Penman-Monteith reference ET from POWER weather, sums rainfall per dekad, calculates deficit (ET − rain), applies the traffic-light rule (green ≤ 0 mm, amber < 30 mm, red ≥ 30 mm), and writes all JSON and GeoJSON output files. When Earth Engine credentials are present, it substitutes FAO WaPOR actual ET automatically.
  4. validate_data.py — enforces the data contract on every push via CI.

A GitHub Action (update-data.yml) re-runs the pipeline weekly, commits the result, and triggers a fresh GitHub Pages deploy. The site is entirely static — no server, no database, nothing that can crash during a demo.

Benefits and intended impact:

  • Agriculture Extension field assistants get a route-planning tool: visit the red union councils first.
  • IWMI researchers get a map showing where to place soil-moisture sensors.
  • University of Agriculture Peshawar students get district-level CSVs for thesis work.
  • Journalists and P&D officials get the first public map of irrigated area in KP.
  • The weekly auto-update means the map outlives the hackathon.

Tools and languages:
Python 3.11 (pipeline), vanilla JavaScript + Leaflet + Three.js (site), HTML/CSS, GitHub Actions (CI/CD and weekly data refresh), Google Earth Engine (optional, for WaPOR ET and WorldCereal crop statistics). No frameworks, no build step, no npm.

Creativity:

  • Historical baseline: each dekad’s deficit is ranked against the same calendar dekad in 2001–2025 (25-year percentile), so a “red” that happens every November is labelled “not unusual for this time of year” while a red that exceeds 90% of historical years is flagged.
  • Honesty-first design: no screen says “farm,” “forecast,” “predict,” “warning,” “drought,” or “shortage.” Every panel shows its source and generation timestamp. Placeholder data is labelled. Validation failures against the census are shown, not hidden.
  • Trilingual: full Urdu and Pashto translations of every interface string, including technical terms like “evapotranspiration” rendered in accessible local language.
  • Self-updating: the Monday Action + data contract + CI validation means a contributor can swap in CHIRPS rainfall or real union-council boundaries without touching the frontend.

Factors considered:

  • KP’s mountain terrain degrades the half-degree NASA POWER rainfall grid; documented and disclosed in every panel.
  • ESA WorldCereal 2021 crop mask is static and misses terraced plots in Dir and Chitral; this is stated on screen and in the validation scatter.
  • The 30 mm/dekad threshold is an uncalibrated project assumption, not a peer-reviewed agronomic value; this is documented in docs/thresholds.md with a validation plan.
  • geoBoundaries ADM3 is tehsils (122), not union councils (~1,000); we keep the data contract’s keys as uc_* so the site does not change when real UC polygons are sourced.
dataRefs: NASA POWER Daily Weather Data (precipitation, temperature, humidity, wind, radiation)
